newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China on target for 30 mln tonne '97 crude imports.
newsitem.headline: China on target for 30 mln tonne '97 crude imports.

text.p: China is on target for crude imports in 1997 of 30 million tonnes -- a substantial rise on 1996, Chinese traders said on Monday.
With more than six months of 1997 gone already, traders said they expected a steady stream of crude imports in the second half.
In the first five months of 1997, China's crude imports totalled 11.71 million tonnes, more than half of the 22.6 million China imported in 1996, according to the State Statistics Bureau.
China is scheduled to announce crude imports for the first six months of 1997 in late July.
Chinese officials have estimated China's crude imports would rise to some 30 million tonnes in 1997, one third greater than the 22.6 million in 1996, thanks to the rapidly growing domestic economy.

"We are importing crude according to our plan in the first six months. There should not be major changes in the import pattern in the second half," said an official with China International United Petroleum and Chemicals Co (Unipec).
Unipec, one of China's main crude importers, plans to import 12 million tonnes of crude oil in 1997, up from nine million in 1996, the official said from Beijing.
The official declined deatils on Unipec's imports in the first six months but said, "We should be able to meet the annual target."
Sources with another major state crude importer, China National Chemicals Imports and Exports Corp (Sinochem), said some coastal refineries had purchased more than their quotas in the first half.

"Some refineries imported more than their quotas in the first half when international crude prices were not that high. They have to adjust their import pace slightly to meet official quotas," said a source with Sinochem.
Surging demand at home as well as improving refining capacity and utilisation also inspired Chinese refineries to import more crude, the source said.
Sinochem plans to import a total of eight million tonnes of crude on its own account in 1997 and imports in the first six months have exceeded four million, he said.
"It should not be a problem even if Sinochem ran out of its quota before the year-end," a Chinese trader said from Beijing.
Separately, Sinochem can also import crude on behalf of Unipec or other state importers in the second half of the year, which will not affect its official quota, the trader said.
Energy analysts have been optimistic about China's crude imports ability in coming years, amid one of the world's fastest growing economies and a lack of new oil reserves at home.

China's gross domestic product (GDP) grew a sizzling 9.7 percent in 1996. It has set an official target of eight percent GDP growth this year, with the first quarter jumping 9.4 percent on a year-on-year basis.
China's annual crude imports could soar to 50 million tonnes by the year 2000, Chinese officials have said.
